opus-5.5.text:
Creativity is one of those words everyone uses but nobody quite agrees on. When people evaluate whether language models are "creative," they often reach for open-ended things like writing poems, generating stories, or brainstorming research ideas. Those are important, but they're incredibly hard to measure. You end up relying on human judgments or on another model acting as a judge. It's very difficult to tell whether a model is doing something new or just remixing something it saw in its enormous training set, which we usually can't inspect.

So my instinct, which comes from how I've approached robustness and generalization more broadly, was to strip the problem down. What are the core ingredients of creativity? Roughly, you need to produce something that's valid, so it satisfies some constraints, and also novel and diverse, so it isn't simply a copy of what you've seen. And often there's a step where you have to make a leap, connecting things in a way that isn't spelled out for you. If you can design small, controlled tasks that capture those ingredients, where you know exactly what the training data contains and you can check precisely whether an output is correct and original, then you can ask sharp scientific questions.

That control lets you go beyond "is this model creative?" You can start asking why it succeeds or fails. Is the training objective the bottleneck? Is it the way we sample at inference time? What happens when you change the architecture or the data? With messy real-world benchmarks, all of those factors get tangled together.

The other motivation is that simple settings often reveal surprisingly fundamental limitations. One thing we've been interested in is whether next-token prediction is the right objective for tasks that need planning or global, "aha"-style thinking. You can see that tension very clearly in a minimal task. In a big open-ended benchmark it would be buried under a lot of noise.

To be clear, I don't think toy tasks are the whole story. The point is that they give you clean hypotheses and insights you can then take back to larger, more realistic settings and test. For me, building that understanding from the ground up is the most reliable way to make progress on something as slippery as creativity.

r001.rationale: It identifies validity, novelty, diversity, and leaps as creativity ingredients, then asks whether next-token prediction is suitable for tasks requiring planning or global insight.

r002.rationale: It says the training set is enormous and usually cannot be inspected, making it difficult to tell whether outputs are new or remixed.

r003.rationale: It explains that controlled, simple tasks let researchers ask whether the training objective is a bottleneck and examine how it affects success or failure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the motivation really came from a frustration with how creativity gets evaluated in language models right now. If you look at a lot of the work out there, it's things like, "Here's a poem the model wrote, does it feel creative?" or "Rate this story on a scale of one to ten." And those evaluations are fundamentally subjective. Two people will disagree, and more importantly, you can't really diagnose anything from them. If the model fails, you don't know why. Is it the training objective? Is it the data? Is it the way we decode? You just have this fuzzy signal.

So my thinking was, if we actually want to understand whether these models can be creative, and what's holding them back, we need tasks where creativity has a precise meaning. That's what led us to these very minimal, almost toy-like settings. Things like, can the model discover a hidden structure, make a novel combination, or produce a diverse set of valid outputs when there are many right answers? In those tasks, you can define exactly what counts as a correct and novel response, and you can measure things like coverage and originality cleanly.

And I'd say this reflects a broader philosophy in how I like to do research. I came from the robustness and adversarial examples world, and one of the lessons there was that when you work on the full messy problem, it's really easy to fool yourself. Simple, controlled settings let you isolate mechanisms. You can ask, what does next-token prediction fundamentally encourage? Does it push toward the most likely continuation at the expense of the interesting one? Does standard autoregressive decoding commit too early to a path?

Once you have those kinds of clean results, they often generalize surprisingly well. We've found that failure modes we see in these tiny tasks show up in the big models too. So the simple tasks aren't a toy for their own sake. They're a kind of lens, a way to get at the first-principles question of what creativity even requires from a learning algorithm, before we go and try to fix it in the wild.

r001.rationale: The response asks what next-token prediction encourages and what creativity requires from a learning algorithm, framing the study around whether training objectives support creativity.

r002.rationale: It mentions data as one possible source of failure, but does not identify uncertainty about models’ training data as an obstacle to interpreting creativity benchmarks.

r003.rationale: It says controlled, concrete tasks isolate mechanisms and let researchers ask what next-token prediction encourages, making objective-related effects on creative performance analyzable.

astra-6.text:
We wanted to make creativity something we could study concretely. When you ask a language model to write a story, it’s difficult to disentangle what’s creative from what’s fluent, what’s familiar, and what you personally like. And if it produces something surprising, it’s hard to know what led to that result.

So we took a step back and asked: what are some basic ingredients of creativity? One is producing something new while still satisfying constraints. Randomness can give you novelty, but that doesn’t necessarily make the result useful or meaningful.

Simple tasks let us isolate that tension. We can make the constraints explicit, look at the range of valid answers, and ask whether the model explores that range or keeps returning to a few familiar solutions. That doesn’t capture everything we mean by creativity, but it gives us a more precise starting point for understanding what these models can do and where they struggle.

r001.rationale: The response describes novelty under constraints as a useful way to study creativity, but does not frame the study as testing whether existing training objectives produce creative capabilities.

r002.rationale: It mentions difficulty interpreting creative outputs, but does not identify uncertainty about the models’ training data as an obstacle.

r003.rationale: It says simple tasks help isolate constraints and explore valid answers, but does not explain how they characterize the effects of different training objectives on creative performance.

sol-6.1.text:
We wanted to make this question of creativity a little more concrete. When you ask whether an LLM can write a creative story, it’s hard to separate what it learned from its training data, how well it follows instructions, and whether it’s actually producing something new. And even evaluating creativity is difficult, because people can disagree about what makes a story creative.

So our approach was to step back and ask: Can we construct simple tasks that capture some ingredients of creativity, where we can precisely define what counts as a valid answer and what counts as a novel one? That gives us a controlled setting to understand what the model is doing and where it struggles. The idea isn’t that these simple tasks capture all of human creativity, but that they let us isolate mechanisms that would be much harder to study in an open-ended setting.

r001.rationale: The response discusses isolating aspects of creativity but does not mention whether existing training objectives produce creativity capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says training data is hard to separate from other factors, but does not identify uncertainty about what data the models were trained on as an obstacle.

r003.rationale: It says simple tasks enable controlled study of model behavior, but does not explain how they characterize the effects of different training objectives on creative performance.
